h1: Keeping a cellar log of the beers you are ageing
title: Keeping a Cellar Log for Aged Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: What to record for every beer you age at home, how to set up a simple cellar log and how to use it to decide when to open a bottle.
teaser: A cellar without a log is a box of guesses. Ten columns in a spreadsheet fix that.
standfirst: Ageing beer only teaches you something if you write it down. Here is the log we would keep: what goes in it, when to update it and how it tells you which bottle to open next.
sections: Memory is the weakest part of any cellar

Put a bottle of barley wine away today and open it in two years. You will remember that you liked it. You will not remember how sweet it was, how hot the alcohol felt or whether that sherry note was there on day one. Without a record, ageing becomes a story you tell yourself.

We work with brewery data for a living and the rule is the same at home as in a brewhouse: an observation you did not write down did not happen. A cellar log turns a shelf of bottles into a slow experiment. It also stops the most common home cellar mistake, which is forgetting a bottle until it is well past its best.

Keep it short enough that you will actually fill it in. One row per bottle:

  • Beer name and brewery.
  • Style and ABV. Most beers worth ageing sit at 8% ABV or above.
  • Packaged-on or bottled date from the label, plus the batch or lot code if there is one.
  • Best-before date, if printed.
  • Where and when you bought it and what you paid.
  • Closure: crown cap, cork and cage or can.
  • Where it sits in your house.
  • Your planned opening date.
  • Tasting notes each time you open one.
  • A score out of 10 for how much you enjoyed it.

The packaged-on date is the field people skip most and the one that matters most. Age is measured from packaging, not from the day you bought it. Our guide to reading packaged-on and best-before dates explains how to find it.

Two identical bottles aged for a year at 13 °C and at 30 °C will taste like different beers. So the log needs a line on conditions, not just dates. Note the room or cupboard, roughly what temperature it holds through the year and anything unusual: a week without power, a move between flats, a bottle that travelled in a car boot.

A cheap digital thermometer with a min and max memory is enough. Check it once a week and write the range in a separate tab. After one Indian summer you will know whether your cupboard is a cellar or an oven. Our guide to cellar temperature and humidity gives the targets.
Write tasting notes you can compare later

Notes are only useful if the next set can be read against them. Use the same order every time: appearance, aroma, flavour, mouthfeel, finish. Serve at the same temperature, around 12 to 14 °C for strong ales, in the same glass. Taste before food.

Write what you find, not what you expect. If you are looking for dried fruit because the label promised it, you will find dried fruit. Short concrete words beat long ones: raisin, toffee, wet paper, warming alcohol. Mark each note with the bottle age in months so you can line them up later.
Read the log like a brewer reads a batch record

In a brewery, nobody judges a batch from one gravity reading. You look at the trend. Treat your cellar the same way. Once a beer has three dated notes, put them side by side and look for direction: sweetness falling, dried fruit rising, carbonation drifting. Three points make a line. One point is an anecdote.

Add a simple column called "trend" with one of three words: improving, holding or fading. Update it after each opening. Over a couple of years that column becomes the most useful thing in the sheet. It shows which styles suit your storage and which breweries make beers that last. It also shows your own habits, such as always opening the best bottles too early.
Use the log to decide when to open

Buy at least three bottles of anything you want to follow. Open the first soon after buying to set a baseline. Open the second at about a year. Your notes then tell you which way the beer is moving. If the sweetness has rounded off and the alcohol has calmed, the third bottle may improve further. If a papery note has crept in, open it soon.

Sort the sheet by planned opening date and look at it once a month. A beer that peaked six months ago in your notes should move to the front of the queue. Hoarding a bottle for a special day is how good beer turns into cardboard.
A spreadsheet beats an app you will abandon

Cellar apps come and go. A spreadsheet on your phone will outlast all of them and you can sort, filter and chart it as the collection grows. Add a column for the shelf position so you can find a bottle without moving twelve others in a warm room.

The gap most people hit is vocabulary. You taste something has changed but cannot name it, so the notes say "different" and teach you nothing. Training your nose to separate oxidation, ester and alcohol notes is what turns a log from a list into a record you can learn from.

Your first step: pick the three bottles you care about most, find their packaged-on dates tonight and start the sheet with those three rows.
faqs: What should a beer cellar log include?
At minimum the beer, ABV, packaged-on date, storage spot, planned opening date and dated tasting notes. Those fields let you track how each beer changes.
Do I need special software to keep a cellar log?
No. A spreadsheet works well and lasts longer than most apps. Keep one row per bottle and a separate tab for storage temperatures.
How often should I taste a beer I am ageing?
For a beer you have several bottles of, open one at the start and then roughly once a year. Compare each note with the last before deciding when to open the next.
